pos: n. (Lorenzo Valla, c. 1407–1457, Italian humanist and papal secretary, who proved the Donation of Constantine a forgery and whose Annotations on the New Testament set Erasmus to work)
etymology: Italian Valla, Latinized Laurentius Valla; Lorenzo from Latin Laurentius, of Laurentum.
biblical_def: Lorenzo Valla was the sharpest philologist of the early Renaissance and used his skill on documents the church had rested on for centuries. In 1440 he demonstrated that the Donation of Constantine — the deed by which the emperor was supposed to have granted the Western empire to the pope — was an eighth-century forgery, exposed by its vocabulary, its anachronisms and its barbarous Latin. He also wrote Annotations comparing the Vulgate with the Greek New Testament, noting where Jerome's Latin had misrendered the original. That manuscript lay forgotten until Erasmus found and printed it in 1505, and from it came the Greek New Testament of 1516 on which the Reformation's exegesis was built. Valla was no Protestant; he served three popes and died a papal secretary. But his principle is the Reformation's: the text as it stands, in the language it was written in, judged by evidence. Pro 12:19 is his vindication — “The lip of truth shall be established for ever: but a lying tongue is but for a moment” — and Eph 4:25 its rule, “putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a forgery as the crime of counterfeiting; and philology as criticism; the study of the structure and derivation of language.
webster_full: FOR'GERY, n. The crime of counterfeiting; the making or alteration of a writing with a view to defraud another.
2. That which is forged, counterfeited or falsely devised.
PHILOL'OGY, n. Criticism; the study and knowledge of languages, their structure and derivation.
scriptures: The lip of truth shall be established for ever: but a lying tongue is but for a moment.
Eph 4:25
Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.
Pro 30:6
Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar.
Deu 4:2
Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.
corruption_summary: A claim that needs a forged deed to support it was never true, and the papal temporal power rested on one for six hundred years.
corruption_paragraphs: The Donation was not a marginal document. It was cited by canonists and popes as the legal title to the Papal States and as an argument for papal superiority over emperors, and it was fraudulent. Valla did not refute the theology; he refuted the paper, and in doing so showed what sort of foundation the claim had. Deu 4:2 is the governing principle for every addition to what God has given: “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it,” and Pro 30:6 adds the warning to the one who adds, “lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar.” An institution that must manufacture its warrant has confessed it has none.

The second matter is the use the same method was later turned to. Textual scholarship of Valla's kind is a servant of the Word, and the Reformers used it gratefully; in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries the identical tools were aimed at Scripture itself, on the assumption that the canon is as much a human construction as the Donation was. The difference is the one Valla himself would have insisted on: evidence. The Donation collapses under examination; the Scriptures do not, and the church may therefore welcome the closest scrutiny of the text while refusing the premise that scrutiny must end in doubt.

“Add thou not unto his words” (Pro 30:6) — the rule the Donation broke.
“Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you” (Deu 4:2) — the standing prohibition.

pos: n. (Francesco Petrarca, 1304–1374, Italian poet and scholar, called the father of humanism, whose recovery of the classical sources set the ad fontes instinct going)
etymology: Italian Petrarca, from Petracco, his father's name, a diminutive of Pietro.
biblical_def: Petrarch hunted manuscripts across Europe, recovered letters of Cicero that no one had read for centuries, and taught his age to go back to the sources rather than to the summaries — the instinct that, applied two centuries later to the Hebrew and Greek Scriptures, produced the Reformation. He is also the first modern man to write about his own interior life at length. The Secretum is a dialogue with Augustine, whose Confessions he carried in his pocket and quoted constantly, and his account of climbing Mont Ventoux ends with him opening that book at random and reading a rebuke of men who admire mountains and neglect themselves. His religion is genuine and unresolved: he knows Ecc 2:11, that “all was vanity and vexation of spirit,” and he cannot let go of the fame he calls vanity. Psa 39:6 describes him exactly — “Surely every man walketh in a vain shew” — and Psa 63:1 names the thirst he felt and could not satisfy by letters. Php 3:13 is the resolution he never quite reached: “forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines humanism by way of the humanities, polite literature; and vanity as emptiness; want of substance to satisfy desire.
webster_full: VAN'ITY, n. Emptiness; want of substance to satisfy desire; uncertainty; inanity.
2. Fruitless desire or endeavor.
3. Empty pleasure; vain pursuit; idle show.
scriptures: Ecc 2:11
Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun.
Psa 39:6
Surely every man walketh in a vain shew: surely they are disquieted in vain: he heapeth up riches, and knoweth not who shall gather them.
Psa 63:1

A Psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Judah. O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is;
Php 3:13
Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before,
corruption_summary: Petrarch is the pattern of the Christian humanist who diagnoses his own vanity with great eloquence and keeps it, which is a condition the modern reader should recognize.
corruption_paragraphs: The Secretum is a remarkable document precisely because its author will not finish the argument. Augustine, in the dialogue, presses him to let go of his desire for glory and of his attachment to Laura; Petrarch agrees in principle and asks for a little more time. That is the religion of the divided man, and Ecc 2:11 is the honest half of it. What is missing is not self-knowledge, of which he has an abundance, but the single thing that can break the tie: a righteousness received, which frees a man from needing to build a name. Diagnosis is not repentance, and eloquence about one's own emptiness can be another way of filling it.

The nearer corruption is the ad fontes principle cut loose from Scripture. Petrarch's return to the sources meant Cicero and Virgil as much as the apostles, and the humanism that descends from him has often made antiquity itself the authority, so that the recovery of ancient texts becomes a cultivation of the self rather than a submission to the Word. The Reformers took his method and changed its object: back to the sources meant back to the Hebrew and the Greek, under the rule of Psa 63:1, a soul that thirsts for God and is told where He may be found.

pos: n. (Johann Reuchlin, 1455–1522, German humanist and the first Christian Hebraist of rank, author of De Rudimentis Hebraicis, who defended the Jewish books against destruction)
etymology: German Reuchlin, a diminutive of Rauch, smoke; he sometimes Graecized himself as Capnion, from kapnos, smoke.
biblical_def: Johann Reuchlin gave the Western church the tools to read the Old Testament in Hebrew. His De Rudimentis Hebraicis of 1506 is a grammar and lexicon together, and he said of it, with justice, that he had raised a monument more lasting than bronze: every Protestant exegete of the next century learned from it or from books built on it, and Luther's Old Testament work was possible because of it. He then faced the test of his life. A converted Jew named Pfefferkorn, backed by the Cologne Dominicans, obtained an imperial order for the seizure and burning of Hebrew books; Reuchlin was asked for an opinion and gave it against the burning, arguing that the Talmud and the rabbinic commentaries should be studied, not destroyed, and that the Jews were fellow citizens with legal rights. The controversy consumed a decade and nearly ruined him. His ground is Rom 3:2, that to the Jews “were committed the oracles of God,” and Rom 11:1, “Hath God cast away his people? God forbid.” Rom 10:1 is the right affection toward them: Paul's “heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Hebrew as the language of the Hebrews; and an oracle, in Scripture, as the communications, revelations or messages delivered by God to prophets.
webster_full: HE'BREW, n. A Hebrew; one of the descendants of Abraham. 2. The Hebrew language.
OR'ACLE, n. In Scripture, the communications, revelations or messages delivered by God to prophets.
2. The sanctuary, or most holy place in the temple.
scriptures: Rom 3:2
Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God.
Rom 11:1
I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid. For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.
Rom 10:1
Brethren, my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved.
Deu 4:2
Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.
corruption_summary: Reuchlin stood against the burning of the Hebrew books, and the church that wanted them burned was proposing to destroy the language of its own Old Testament.
corruption_paragraphs: The proposal to burn the Jewish books was the fruit of a long and wicked tradition, and it was also self-defeating: a church that destroys Hebrew learning cannot read Moses. Reuchlin's defence rested on both grounds, the justice owed to his neighbours and the usefulness of the books to Christian scholarship, and Rom 3:2 is the deeper reason — the oracles of God were committed to this people, and the Christian who despises them despises the vessel of his own Scriptures. The medieval persecution of the Jews is to be named as sin, not explained as a product of its age.

Reuchlin's own weakness lay elsewhere. He was an enthusiast for the Kabbalah, believing that its mysteries confirmed Christian doctrine and that the divine names held hidden power, and he wrote two books arguing it. That is not Hebrew scholarship but occult speculation, and Deu 4:2 forbids the addition: what God has commanded is not supplemented by a secret tradition. The recovery is to take the grammar and leave the mysticism, and to hold toward the Jewish people the affection of Rom 10:1 rather than either the contempt of his opponents or the credulity of his own Kabbalism.

roots_lines: Greek logion (G3051) — an oracle, a divine saying; Romans 3:2.
Greek apotheomai (G683) — to cast away, to reject; Romans 11:1.

Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, a matter; Deuteronomy 4:2.

“Hath God cast away his people? God forbid” (Rom 11:1) — against the burners.

pos: n. (the Complutensian Polyglot, printed at Alcalá 1514–1517 and published 1522 under Cardinal Jiménez de Cisneros, the first printed Bible setting the original languages in parallel columns)
etymology: Latin Complutum, the Roman name of Alcalá de Henares; polyglot from Greek polus, many, and glotta, tongue.
biblical_def: The Complutensian Polyglot was the great scholarly monument of Spanish humanism. Cardinal Jiménez founded the university at Alcalá, gathered Hebrew, Greek and Latin scholars, bought and borrowed manuscripts, and had new Greek type cut for the purpose. The Old Testament runs in three columns — Hebrew, Vulgate and Septuagint with an interlinear Latin — with the Aramaic Targum of the Pentateuch and its Latin below; the New Testament gives Greek and Vulgate side by side, and the sixth volume provides a Hebrew lexicon and grammar. The Greek New Testament was printed in 1514, two years before Erasmus, but publication waited on papal permission until 1522, so Erasmus's edition reached the world first and became the basis of the Textus Receptus. The work proceeds on the conviction of Psa 119:160, “Thy word is true from the beginning,” and of Isa 40:8, “the word of our God shall stand for ever.” Psa 12:6 describes what such labour is for: “The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a polyglot as having or containing many languages; as a polyglot lexicon or Bible; and a version as a translation.
webster_full: POL'YGLOT, a. Having or containing many languages; as a polyglot lexicon or Bible.
POL'YGLOT, n. A book containing many languages, particularly the Bible containing the Scriptures in several languages.
VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.
scriptures: Thy word is true from the beginning: and every one of thy righteous judgments endureth for ever.
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.
Psa 12:6
The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
corruption_summary: Rome produced the finest scholarly Bible of the age and then kept it from the people, which is the whole argument of the Reformation in one volume.
corruption_paragraphs: Six hundred sets were printed, in six folio volumes, for scholars and libraries. There was no Spanish translation, and within a few years the Inquisition was burning vernacular Scriptures and prosecuting those who owned them. The Complutensian is therefore a double witness: that Rome was capable of magnificent reverence for the text, and that it did not follow from such reverence that the ploughman should be allowed to read it. The Reformation's complaint was never that Rome neglected scholarship; it was that the Word was withheld, and Mat 24:35 — “my words shall not pass away” — is spoken of words meant to be heard.

A second and modern corruption runs the other way, in the suggestion that a multiplicity of versions and variants makes the text uncertain, so that no translation may be trusted and the believer is left with scholarly opinion. The Polyglot is the standing answer. Set the Hebrew, the Greek, the Septuagint, the Targum and the Latin side by side — which is what Jiménez did, four centuries before the modern apparatus — and what appears is not confusion but a text preserved. Psa 119:160 is not a hope but a finding, confirmed by exactly the comparison this book made possible.
roots_summary: Hebrew emeth (H571), truth; tsaraph (H6884), to refine, to try as metal; Greek parerchomai (G3928), to pass away.
roots_lines: Hebrew emeth (H571) — truth, firmness; Psalm 119:160.
Hebrew tsaraph (H6884) — to refine, to try in a furnace; Psalm 12:6.
Hebrew qum (H6965) — to stand, to arise; Isaiah 40:8.
Greek parerchomai (G3928) — to pass by, to pass away; Matthew 24:35.
Greek glossa (G1100) — tongue, language.

“the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) — why such labour is warranted.
“The words of the LORD are pure words” (Psa 12:6) — the text the Polyglot set out to display.

pos: n. (Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, c. 1455–1536, French humanist and biblical commentator, leader of the Meaux circle and translator of the French New Testament of 1523)
etymology: French Lefèvre, the smith, from Latin faber; Étaples in Picardy, his birthplace. Latinized Faber Stapulensis.
biblical_def: Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples published a commentary on the Pauline epistles in 1512, five years before the Ninety-Five Theses, and in it he taught that a man is justified by faith and not by his works, that merit is a word with no proper place in the doctrine of salvation, and that the righteousness by which we stand is Christ's and not our own. Rom 3:28 is his conclusion as it is Paul's — “Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” — with Rom 4:5 on the God who “justifieth the ungodly” and Rom 10:4 on Christ as “the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth.” Under Bishop Brionnet he led the reforming circle at Meaux, preached the gospel in the diocese, and translated the New Testament and the Psalms into French so that the people could read them. When the Sorbonne moved against the circle he fled to Strasbourg, then returned under the protection of Marguerite of Navarre and died in her household at Nérac, never having left the Roman communion.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a commentary as a comment; exposition; explanation or illustration of the meaning of a writing; and to justify, in theology, as to pardon and clear from guilt.
webster_full: COM'MENTARY, n. A comment; exposition; explanation or illustration of the meaning of a writing.
JUS'TIFY, v.t. In theology, to pardon and clear from guilt; to absolve or acquit from guilt and merited punishment.
2. To prove or show to be just, or conformable to law, right, justice or duty.
scriptures: Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
Gal 2:16

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
Rom 10:4
For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth.
corruption_summary: Lefevre found justification by faith in Paul and could not bring himself to follow it out of Rome, which is the predicament of every evangelical who stays where the gospel is denied.
corruption_paragraphs: Lefèvre's case is the sharpest form of a real question. He held the doctrine, preached it, printed the Scriptures for the people, and remained in a church whose official teaching anathematized what he taught; when pressed he withdrew rather than divided. Sympathy is owed to a man of seventy-five under threat of fire, and so is clarity: Gal 2:16 is not a private opinion but the gospel, and a communion that condemns it is not a communion a man may rest in. Calvin, who met him, drew the conclusion Lefèvre would not, and wrote against the Nicodemites who kept the faith in secret while conforming outwardly.

The second corruption is the modern reading that makes him a model of irenic reform — proof that one may hold evangelical doctrine and avoid the unpleasantness of separation. The Meaux experiment answers it: the circle was broken up, its preachers scattered, one of its number burned, and the diocese returned to what it had been. Rom 3:28 cannot be held quietly where it is forbidden, because it is the article on which a man's standing before God depends, and silence about it is not peace but a withholding of the only news that saves.

roots_lines: Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to justify, to declare righteous; Romans 3:28, Galatians 2:16.
Greek ergon (G2041) — a work, a deed; Romans 3:28.
Greek asebes (G765) — ungodly; Romans 4:5.
Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, to count; Romans 4:5.

“him that justifieth the ungodly” (Rom 4:5) — the God of the gospel.
“Christ is the end of the law for righteousness” (Rom 10:4) — the righteousness that is not ours.

pos: n. (Guillaume Briçonnet, c. 1470–1534, bishop of Meaux, patron of the reforming circle there, who drew back and silenced his own preachers under pressure from the Sorbonne)
etymology: French Briçonnet, a family name of the Touraine; Guillaume, the French form of William.
biblical_def: Guillaume Briçonnet came to the see of Meaux in 1516 determined to reform it. He visited his parishes, found the clergy ignorant and absent, and brought in Lefèvre d'Étaples, Guillaume Farel, Gérard Roussel and others to preach; he divided the diocese into preaching stations, encouraged the French New Testament, and corresponded with Marguerite of Navarre about the gospel in terms no one could mistake. Then the Sorbonne and the Parlement of Paris moved, the Franciscans he had displaced complained, and the king who had shielded him was captured at Pavia. Briçonnet gave way. In 1525 he submitted, condemned Luther's books in his diocese, forbade the circle to preach, and ended his life a conforming bishop while Farel fled to Switzerland and Berquin went to the fire. Pro 29:25 is his epitaph — “The fear of man bringeth a snare” — and Joh 12:43 its diagnosis: “For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a snare as anything by which one is entangled and brought into trouble; and to temporize as to comply with the time or occasion; to yield to the current of opinion.
webster_full: SNARE, n. An instrument for catching animals, particularly birds; a gin; a net.
2. Any thing by which one is entangled and brought into trouble.
TEM'PORIZE, v.i. To comply with the time or occasion; to humor or yield to the current of opinion.
scriptures: The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.
For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.
Gal 2:12
For before that certain came from James, he did eat with the Gentiles: but when they were come, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision.
Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended.
corruption_summary: Briconnet is the reforming patron who folded, and the lesson is that patronage is not conviction and withdraws when the cost arrives.
corruption_paragraphs: The Meaux circle collapsed not because its doctrine was refuted but because its protector calculated. Briçonnet had everything a reform needs except willingness to lose — a diocese, scholars, a press, royal favour — and when the favour went, so did he. Mat 13:21 describes the ground exactly: “Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended.” Even an apostle felt the pull; Gal 2:12 records Peter withdrawing “fearing them which were of the circumcision,” and Paul withstood him to the face for it.

The entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is older and plainer. A church reformed from the top by a patron's goodwill is reformed only as long as the goodwill lasts, which is why the Reformation went forward where it took root in congregations and ministers who had counted the cost. Pro 29:25 gives the alternative in its second clause: “but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.” The men Briçonnet silenced had that trust, and their work survived his.

pos: n. (Louis de Berquin, c. 1490–1529, Picard nobleman and scholar, the first French Reformation martyr of gentle birth, burned in Paris in April 1529)
etymology: French Berquin, from his estate in Artois; Louis, Germanic Hludwig, famous warrior.
biblical_def: Louis de Berquin was a gentleman of Artois, a scholar of the Meaux circle, and a man Erasmus liked and feared for. He translated pieces of Luther and Melanchthon into French, wrote against the invocation of the Virgin and the saints, and argued that the Scriptures should be read by the laity. The Sorbonne condemned his books in 1523 and he was arrested; Marguerite of Navarre and Francis I intervened and he was released. He was arrested again in 1526 and again freed by the king. Erasmus wrote begging him to be quiet. He would not: on his third arrest, in 1529, with the king absent and the Parlement determined, he refused to recant, was degraded, and was strangled and burned in the Place de Grève the same day, before any appeal could reach the court. “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10) is the word spoken to such men. “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Php 1:21) is the arithmetic he accepted. And to friends who urged caution the apostle himself answered, “I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus” (Act 21:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a martyr as one who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel; one who suffers death in defense of any opinion.
webster_full: M'ARTYR, n. One who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel.
2. One who suffers death in defense of any cause.
M'ARTYRDOM, n. The death of a martyr; the suffering of death on account of adherence to the Christian faith.
scriptures: Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Php 1:21
For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
Then Paul answered, What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart? for I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
corruption_summary: Berquin was told three times by wiser friends to be quiet, and the quietness they urged would have cost France its first witness.
corruption_paragraphs: Erasmus's advice was prudent, affectionate and wrong. He had spent his life proving that criticism could be made safely by being made obliquely, and he genuinely could not see why a man would speak plainly at the price of burning. But the question Berquin faced was not one of tactics: he was required to say that the invocation of saints is lawful and that the laity should not read the Scriptures, and to say it would have been to deny what he knew. Act 21:13 is the pattern of answer to friends who weep and urge caution, and Paul gave it on the road to a city he knew would bind him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, and the principle to recover is the distinction between prudence and compromise. There is a time to withdraw — the apostles left cities, Paul went over a wall in a basket — and there is a point at which silence is itself a denial, because the thing demanded is a confession. 2Ti 4:7 is the only verdict a man finally wants: “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.” Berquin was thirty-nine and had a estate and a king's favour to lose, and he kept it.

usage: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10) — the word to such men.
“For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Php 1:21) — the arithmetic he accepted.
“I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die” (Act 21:13) — the answer to friends urging caution.

pos: n. (Marguerite d'Angoulême, 1492–1549, queen of Navarre and sister of Francis I, protector of the French evangelicals and author of the Mirror of the Sinful Soul)
etymology: French Marguerite, from Greek margarites, a pearl; Navarre, the kingdom on both slopes of the western Pyrenees.
biblical_def: Marguerite of Navarre stood between the French evangelicals and the fire for twenty-five years, and a great many of them lived because she did. Sister to the king and able to reach him when no one else could, she sheltered Lefèvre d'Étaples in her household until he died, obtained the release of Berquin twice, protected Roussel and Marot, and kept correspondence with the Meaux circle on the doctrine of grace. Her own Miroir de l'âme pécheresse was condemned by the Sorbonne in 1533 and is a long meditation on the soul's helplessness and Christ's sufficiency; Psa 51:17 is its register, “a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise,” and Rom 7:24 its cry, “O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” Her commission is Est 4:14, the word to a queen with access to a king: “who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” and Pro 31:8, “Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction.” She never separated from Rome.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a patron as one who countenances, supports or protects; and intercession as prayer or solicitation to one party in favor of another.
webster_full: PA'TRON, n. A protector; one who countenances or supports; a defender.
INTERCES'SION, n. The act of interceding; mediation; interposition between parties at variance, with a view to reconcilation.
2. Prayer or solicitation to one party in favor of another.
scriptures: Est 4:14

For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?
Pro 31:8
Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction.
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.
Rom 7:24
O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?
corruption_summary: Marguerite used her place at court exactly as Esther used hers, and the modern reading that reduces her to a literary patron misses what she was for.
corruption_paragraphs: She is studied now chiefly as an author and a patron of letters, the writer of the Heptameron and a figure in the French Renaissance, with her religion treated as a period colouring. That inverts her life. The evangelical cause in France had no legal standing and no army; what it had was a woman with the king's ear, and she spent that access on prisoners, preachers and printers. Est 4:14 is the pattern, and it is a pattern of office rightly used: God puts people where they are, and the question put to Esther is the question put to anyone with access — whether it was given for such a time as this.

The honest account must also name what she did not do. Marguerite held the doctrine of grace and remained in the Roman church, protecting men whose convictions she shared without ever confessing them in a way that would cost her; Calvin wrote to her sharply about the Libertines she tolerated. Pro 31:8 was obeyed and the further step was not taken. Her true honour is that she opened her mouth for those appointed to destruction, which is more than most at that court did, and the limitation is that a protector inside the system can save men without reforming the church.

pos: n. (Renée of France, 1510–1575, daughter of Louis XII and duchess of Ferrara, who sheltered Calvin and the persecuted and held the Reformed faith against husband, son and Inquisition)
etymology: French Renée, from Latin renata, born again — a name her life made apt; Ferrara, the duchy of the Este in northern Italy.
biblical_def: Renée of Ferrara was married at twenty to Ercole d'Este and turned her court into a refuge. Calvin visited her in 1536 under the name Charles d'Espeville and corresponded with her for the rest of his life; Clement Marot, Vittoria Colonna and many lesser fugitives found shelter there. Her husband, under pressure from Rome and from his own political need, had her examined, separated her from her children, and in 1554 confined her until she made an outward submission. She did not change. Widowed in 1559 she returned to France, settled at Montargis, and opened it to Huguenot refugees after the massacres, refusing a royal order to surrender them and telling the commander that she would stand in the gate herself. Heb 13:2 was her practice — “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” — and Mat 25:35, “I was a stranger, and ye took me in.” Heb 11:25 names the choice she made at twenty and kept at sixty: “Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hospitality as the act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward, or with kind and generous liberality.
webster_full: HOSPITAL'ITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward, or with kind and generous liberality.
REF'UGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress.
2. That which shelters or protects from danger, distress or calamity.
scriptures: Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:
Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season;
The Lord give mercy unto the house of Onesiphorus; for he oft refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain:
corruption_summary: Hospitality is treated now as a style of entertaining; in Renee's hands it was a capital offence, which is nearer the New Testament meaning.
corruption_paragraphs: The New Testament commands hospitality in a world where receiving the wrong guest could cost a household everything, and that is the setting of Heb 13:2 and of Paul's thanks for Onesiphorus, who “was not ashamed of my chain” (2Ti 1:16). Renée's Montargis was called the hotel of God by the refugees who reached it, and she kept it open against a royal command. The modern domestication of the word — hospitality as a gift for hosting — empties it of the risk that gave it meaning. Mat 25:35 puts the stranger taken in among the deeds the King will own at the judgment.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the duty of shelter, and Renée's life also answers a narrower error. She was pressed for decades by husband, son, confessors and inquisitors, made one forced outward submission under confinement, and went straight back to the faith when she was free — which is why Calvin, who rebuked her freely on other matters, never doubted her. Heb 11:25 describes a choice made once and then made again every year for fifty-five years, and that is what perseverance looks like from inside a life.

pos: n. (Antoine de Chandieu, 1534–1591, French Reformed pastor and theologian, a framer of the Gallican Confession and the first to turn scholastic method to Reformed polemics)
etymology: French Chandieu, from his seigneury in the Dauphiné; he wrote also under the names Sadeel and Zamariel.
biblical_def: Antoine de Chandieu was converted at Paris, pastored the perilous underground congregation there, and at twenty-five helped frame the Gallican Confession adopted by the first national synod of the French Reformed churches in 1559. He survived the massacre of 1572 by flight, served the church in Geneva and Lausanne, acted as chaplain to Henry of Navarre in the field, and died at Geneva. His importance in the history of doctrine is methodological: writing against Bellarmine and the Jesuit controversialists, he argued that Reformed theology must answer scholastic argument in its own form, with careful distinctions and syllogism, and he is the pioneer of what became Reformed scholasticism. The warrant is Tit 1:9, that an elder must hold “the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers,” and 2Ti 1:13, “Hold fast the form of sound words.” 1Ti 6:12 gives the temper of his life: “Fight the good fight of faith.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines polemic as controversial; disputative; and sound doctrine, in theology, as that which is orthodox, true, and conformable to Scripture.
webster_full: POLEM'IC, a. Controversial; disputative; as a polemic treatise or essay.
POLEM'IC, n. A disputant; a controvertist; one who writes in support of an opinion in opposition to another.
SOUND, a. Orthodox; correct; free from error; as a sound divine; sound doctrine.
scriptures: Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: Reformed scholasticism is dismissed now as a cold decline from the Reformers, and Chandieu shows why it was undertaken and what it was for.
corruption_paragraphs: A long-standing caricature treats the generation after Calvin as having traded living faith for arid system, and Chandieu is the answer. He was a hunted pastor who had buried church members, a soldier's chaplain, and a man who adopted precise definition because Bellarmine was precise and vagueness was losing souls. Tit 1:9 requires an elder to be “able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers,” and convincing a trained Jesuit requires training. Method is not coldness; it is the form that care takes when the opponent is competent.

The nearer corruption is the modern evangelical suspicion of doctrinal precision as such — the preference for warmth over definition, as though the two were rivals. 2Ti 1:13 commands that we “hold fast the form of sound words,” and a form is exactly what Chandieu laboured to supply. A church without it cannot defend its people, because every error arrives dressed in the vocabulary of piety. Act 20:28 charges the elder to “feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood,” and feeding includes fencing.
